mula_devanagari: अध्यात्म-ज्ञान-नित्यत्वं तत्त्व-ज्ञानार्थ-दर्शनम् | एतज् ज्ञानम् इति प्रोक्तम् अज्ञानं यद् अतो ऽन्यथा
mula_iast: adhyātma-jñāna-nityatvaṃ tattva-jñānārtha-darśanam | etaj jñānam iti proktam ajñānaṃ yad ato 'nyathā
jayatirtha_prameyadipika: ।।13.12।।ननु तत्त्वज्ञानार्थदर्शनं नाम ज्ञानमेव? तत्कथं ज्ञानसाधनेषूच्यते इत्यत आह -- तत्त्वे ति। शास्त्रदर्शनं तात्पर्यालोचनम्। अत्र शास्त्रस्येत्यध्याहृत्य व्याख्यानमिति ज्ञातव्यम्।

current_dvaita_rendering.english: Tattva-jñānārtha-darśana is the study of scripture for the sake of aparokṣa-jñāna (direct knowledge).
current_dvaita_rendering.divergence_note: THIN: Madhva glosses only one compound, but distinctively: the 'seeing' is śāstra-darśana aimed at aparokṣa-jñāna, making scriptural study the means to direct knowledge, rather than Śaṅkara's contemplation of mokṣa as fruit.

current_dvaita_everyday: An engineer wanting real understanding of a hard domain commits to reading the primary sources slowly, aiming for first-hand grasp rather than secondhand summary - study pointed at direct knowledge.

other_schools_english.advaita: Adhyātma-jñāna-nityatva is constancy in knowledge whose object is the Self; tattva-jñānārtha-darśana is keeping in view the fruit of tattva-jñāna (knowledge of reality), which ripens from long practice of amānitva and the rest - that fruit being mokṣa, the cessation of saṃsāra - for one who contemplates the fruit is moved to practise its means. All this, from amānitva up to this, is called jñāna because it is for the sake of knowledge, and what is contrary - pride, ostentation, violence, impatience, crookedness - is to be known as ajñāna, so that it may be avoided as the cause of saṃsāra. If one objects that these are yamas and niyamas that cannot reveal any object as knowledge does, the reply is that they are called knowledge as its causes and auxiliaries.
other_schools_english.viśiṣṭādvaita: Adhyātma-jñāna is knowledge of the self, and nityatva is being established in it; tattva-jñānārtha-darśana is being devoted to the reality that is the purpose of knowing truth. 'Jñāna' here means that by which the self is known, the means to self-knowledge: the cluster of qualities, amānitva and the rest, of the puruṣa connected with the kṣetra alone helps self-knowledge, while everything else is a product of the kṣetra opposed to it and so is ajñāna. Next, the nature of the kṣetrajña, introduced earlier as the knower, is to be purified and set out.
other_schools_english.śuddhādvaita: This knowledge that has been declared is the work of vidyā; what is otherwise is ajñāna, the work of avidyā.
other_schools_english.bhakti: Adhyātma-jñāna is knowledge that concerns the Self, and constancy in it means steadfastness in purifying the meaning of the word 'tvam' (you). Tattva-jñānārtha-darśana is looking at the purpose of knowledge of reality, mokṣa, as the highest of all. These twenty, beginning with amānitva, are called knowledge as its means, and their opposites are called ignorance, as by Vasiṣṭha and others, because they oppose knowledge - so they are to be abandoned entirely.
other_schools_english.advaita-bhakti: Adhyātma-jñāna is discrimination of Self from non-Self, and constancy is being established in it, for one established in discrimination becomes able to know the meaning of the great sentence. Tattva-jñāna is the direct realization 'I am Brahman', produced by Vedānta sentences as the ripened fruit of all the means; its purpose is mokṣa - the cessation of all sorrow, avidyā and its effects, and the attainment of the Self as supreme bliss - and seeing it moves one to practise the means. These twenty, ending here, are called knowledge for its sake, and pride and the rest, their opposite, ignorance as its obstacle; therefore abandon ignorance and take up knowledge alone.
